title: Certified Raw Milk: Testing, Herdshares, Insurance
one_liner: The neutral assurance layer for the gray-legal raw milk market: weekly pathogen and H5N1 testing, herdshare paperwork, and the first insurable 'tested farm' program.
customer: Small dairies (roughly 5-100 cows) that sell raw milk through herdshares or state-permitted on-farm sales. Later, surplus-lines insurers and MGAs, and consumers who scan a batch QR code.
problem: Demand for raw milk is rising with the wellness and MAHA-era food politics, but farms run with no shared safety standard, no liability coverage, and thin legal paperwork. Herdshares are a legal workaround that state attorneys general and FDA (on interstate sales) increasingly scrutinize as disguised retail. H5N1 in dairy herds since 2024 and USDA's national milk-testing strategy raised the stakes. One sick customer can end a farm.
solution: A subscription with four parts. (1) Scheduled bulk-tank sampling, with a partner state-accredited lab running a pathogen panel (Salmonella, Listeria, STEC, Campylobacter) plus H5N1 PCR. (2) A public farm page and batch QR code that show results, including failures. (3) State-specific herdshare agreements and an incident-response protocol, reviewed by counsel. (4) After 6-12 months of data, a group liability policy priced off each farm's test history.
why_now: H5N1 in US dairy cattle (2024-26) made pathogen testing a mainstream topic. Federal and state milk-testing programs are expanding. Raw milk politics are at a high, and 2026 reporting shows FDA pressure on interstate sales and closer AG review of herdshare contracts. Farms now need a defensible paper trail, and insurers have no data to price this risk.
revenue_model: $150-400 per farm per month for testing and certification, with lab costs around 40%. Per-batch certificate fees. A 10-15% commission or MGA fee on group liability premiums once claims data exists. Optional $5/month 'verified member' fee paid by herdshare customers.
non_obvious_insight: Raw milk's growth is capped by trust and insurability, not demand. Insurers, retailers and regulators won't touch it because nobody can prove anything. The winner is not a milk brand but the certifier (think UL or organic certification) that publishes failures. Believers and skeptics can both trust that, and the test history becomes the underwriting dataset that unlocks insurance, which is the real moat.
first_30_days: Pick one state with a strong raw-milk farmer network and clear legal footing (for example Pennsylvania or Utah). Recruit 10-15 farms through state raw-milk associations and Farm-to-Consumer Legal Defense Fund events. Sign a wholesale rate with an accredited lab. Sell a $199/month 'weekly test plus public results page' pilot. Show 3 months of data to 2 surplus-lines brokers to scope a group liability program.

title: Rent Seasonal Nitrate Treatment, Don't Build Plants
one_liner: Trailer-mounted nitrate-removal skids rented to small farm-belt utilities only for the 60-120 days a year when river or shallow-well nitrate spikes.
customer: Small and mid-size utilities (500-10,000 people) in Iowa, Nebraska, Illinois, Minnesota, Kansas and Wisconsin that draw from rivers or shallow aquifers. Systems with recent nitrate MCL violations are first. The utility pays, and state programs may help.
problem: More than 60M Americans are served from elevated-nitrate sources, and the 10 ppm limit dates from 1991. EPA's cancer review has stalled since 2023, and its research office is gone. Small rural systems bear treatment costs alone. A permanent $2-10M plant is out of reach for them, though the exceedance is seasonal.
solution: A fleet of containerized nitrate-selective ion-exchange skids sized 0.25-2 MGD. Include resin regeneration, brine logistics (the make-or-break piece, so pre-agree the disposal route with the wastewater plant or a hauler), operator training and remote monitoring. Priced as a seasonal service, per 1,000 gallons treated with a seasonal minimum. Start asset-light by leasing skids from an existing ion-exchange OEM.
why_now: Federal action on nitrate is stalled, so relief is not coming from Washington. Broad drought followed by heavy runoff swings nitrate hard. The FY2026 $7.2B SRF pool makes states receptive to flexible compliance solutions. The 10 ppm limit is still enforceable today.
revenue_model: Seasonal rental of $15-40k/month per skid plus per-gallon regeneration and brine fees, under 3-5 year master service agreements.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume compliance means permanent capital. But nitrate is a peak problem (Des Moines Water Works runs its removal plant only during high-nitrate stretches, from my background knowledge), so the winning model sells the peak, not the plant. A rental converts an unfundable capital project into a fundable operating line.
first_30_days: Pull three years of nitrate MCL violations from the public SDWIS database and build a list of 100 systems. Call five directly and through a state rural water association. Sign an MOU with one ion-exchange OEM for lease-back skids, and get one utility to agree to a paid pilot for spring 2027.

title: China-Asset Diligence Desk for Pharma BD
one_liner: A bilingual scientist-plus-software sprint that verifies China-sourced drug packages (raw data, GLP and CMC standing, ownership chain) in 72 hours for US buyers.
customer: Pharma BD&L teams, NewCo-building VCs, royalty funds and mid-cap biotechs in-licensing Chinese assets.
problem: About one-third of 2025 licensing spend involved China-sourced drugs (Jefferies) and the pace accelerated in 2026 (Lilly-InnoCare up to $3.35B, Merck-SciBrunch $2.1B). Diligence infrastructure looks thin (inference): data packages are in Chinese formats, raw-data and audit-trail norms differ, and CRO and CDMO GLP or GMP standing is hard to verify. BIOSECURE, enacted Dec 18, 2025, requires OMB to publish the list of biotechnology companies of concern by December 2026 and FAR rules follow, adding an ownership and supply-chain axis.
solution: A fixed-price 'Asset Verification Sprint'. LLM-assisted translation and structured extraction of study reports. Bilingual scientists spot-check raw data and audit trails. Verify CRO and CDMO inspection histories (NMPA, FDA, EMA) and check ownership chains against the BIOSECURE lists. Deliver a Western-format gap analysis for IND-enabling needs (GLP tox acceptability, CMC comparability).
why_now: Deal flow is at record levels, BIOSECURE list publication is due in about three months, and biopharma layoffs (15,000+) free bilingual ex-pharma scientists.
revenue_model: $25-70k per sprint, $150-300k annual retainers for NewCo-builder VCs, and supply-chain mapping as a second product once the BIOSECURE lists land.
non_obvious_insight: The gap is not legal or financial diligence. It is data literacy and tacit standards, for example what counts as GLP-grade raw data, and Western deal associates cannot read the packages. The same team and database serve a second product, supply-chain mapping, when the lists arrive.
first_30_days: Recruit 3-4 bilingual ex-pharma scientists. Price a $20k pilot sprint. Approach 5 NewCo VC platforms and 5 mid-size pharma BD heads. Build a CRO and CDMO inspection database from public regulator records.

title: Volumetric Concert Replays for Small Venues
one_liner: A multi-camera Gaussian-splat capture rig that lets attendees of 200-2,000 capacity shows buy a free-viewpoint replay of their favorite songs.
customer: Independent venues, promoters and mid-tier touring acts, with ticket-holders as end buyers at $5-15 per replay.
problem: Small acts earn only from tickets and merch, and concert film needs a crew. Sphere grossed $420.5M in 2024 but is for superstars. Fans want to relive the night from where they stood, and no affordable product delivers it.
solution: A 12-24 camera synced rig hung on lighting truss, cloud splat processing, and a phone and headset web viewer. Attendees unlock replays via a ticket QR code. Start with one or two songs with static cameras and add motion later, with revenue shared with the venue and artist.
why_now: 4D Gaussian splatting hit practical quality and cost in 2025-26, web viewers are mature, and headsets are common enough to matter.
revenue_model: $2-5k capture fee per show or free capture with 50% of replay sales, plus venue subscription for archives.
non_obvious_insight: The asset is not the film but the fan's own position. Selling 'the replay from where I stood' to the 300 people who attended targets a captive small market with high willingness to pay.
first_30_days: Build a 12-camera rig for about $8k. Capture 3 local shows in exchange for rights. Test QR-code replay sales at the merch table and measure conversion.

title: Roll Up the Layer Under Funeral Homes
one_liner: Instead of buying funeral homes, buy the removal services and wholesale crematories that independent homes depend on, and run them with AI dispatch, chain-of-custody and paperwork agents.
customer: Independent funeral homes, roughly 60% to 70% of which have no crematory of their own, plus hospice and medical-examiner contractors. Families are indirect beneficiaries.
problem: Consolidators are buying the retail funeral homes that families see, and independents are squeezed. Independents struggle to staff 24/7 first-call removals, outsource cremation to small crematories with uneven chain-of-custody, and lose days chasing physician signatures in state electronic death registration systems. Families cannot see where their loved one is.
solution: Buy regional removal companies and wholesale crematories from retiring owners. AI ops layer: a dispatch agent for 3 a.m. first calls and routing, barcode and photo chain-of-custody at every handoff with a family-facing status link (like package tracking), a paperwork agent that chases physician and ME signatures and files EDRS entries, permits and cremation authorizations, and capacity balancing across retorts. Sell independents a per-case bundle that lets them offer end-to-end service without capital or overnight staff.
why_now: Independent homes face consolidation pressure and the shift to cremation, and overnight labor is scarce. States are modernizing death-registration workflows (for example Michigan's March 2026 HB 4077 and 4078), and voice and browser agents can now do first-call dispatch and portal filing.
revenue_model: $150 to $300 per removal, $250 to $450 per wholesale cremation, and $50 to $100 per case for paperwork. A typical home with 150 cases per year yields $60k to $120k of annual revenue.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone is buying the storefront. The stickier profit pools are the invisible utilities behind thousands of small homes, and the hard parts (3 a.m. dispatch, custody proof, signature chasing) are exactly what AI operations do well. Serving independents also positions the roll-up as their ally against consolidators.
first_30_days: Ride along with one or two removal services. Offer five funeral homes a 'paperwork chaser' that monitors EDRS status and emails doctors, at about $60 per case. Then buy or partner with the removal company serving them, using seller notes. Build the family status link early and let funeral directors show it to families.

title: Tip Provenance Ledger for Tipped-Occupation Employers
one_liner: An evidence trail that classifies every dollar as a voluntary tip, service charge, pool or cash tip, to support new tip-deduction reporting.
customer: Restaurants, bars, salons, spas, barbershops, valet operators, car washes and delivery fleets with 5-60 workers on Toast, Square, Clover or spreadsheets, and self-employed booth renters in tipped occupations.
problem: The 2025 reconciliation law made qualified tips and overtime deductible, and the IRS says employers must file information returns on them. Workers now have an incentive to relabel pay as tips. Owners must separate voluntary tips from mandatory service charges, pooled tips and cash tips, and errors trigger worker disputes and IRS letters.
solution: Ingest POS, payment and payroll data and tag each dollar with provenance. Produce the W-2 or 1099 support schedule, worker-facing statements so employees can claim their deduction, and an audit binder. Flag anomalies such as a service charge quietly recategorized as tips at year-end.
why_now: Tax year 2026 is the first full year under the new rules and W-2s are due January 31, 2027. Payroll vendors are adding fields but not provenance.
revenue_model: $29-79 per location per month, plus $3 per worker statement. Channel through POS app stores and restaurant bookkeepers.
non_obvious_insight: A deduction that is valuable to both worker and owner creates an incentive to reclassify, which makes the evidence trail the product, in the same way that exemption certificates support sales-tax deductions. Payroll vendors will add a field but not the audit trail.
first_30_days: Recruit 15 restaurants and salons through bookkeepers. Build a Square and Toast CSV importer and offer a free Q4 tip audit. Convert audit customers to an annual plan ahead of the W-2 deadline.

title: Tamper-Proof Photo Evidence for Produce Rejections
one_liner: A capture-only app that produces AI-proof receiving-dock photo and video evidence so shippers can contest bogus load rejections and reroute rejected produce to salvage buyers within hours.
customer: Mid-size grower-shippers and brokers of berries, leafy greens, tomatoes and other perishables (Salinas, Yuma, Nogales and Florida corridors). PACA-licensed receivers who want to prove genuine rejections are a second segment, and produce factoring companies a third.
problem: Produce is sold before it arrives, and when market prices fall, a rejection on 'condition' photos is a well-known way to force a price cut. Shippers have photos, phone calls and slow inspections. Generative editing makes photos cheap to fabricate or alter, and neither side can prove authenticity (IC3 notes many victims cannot tell AI was involved). Rejected loads then rot or are dumped because salvage rerouting is slow, adding to food waste.
solution: In-app capture only, with device attestation, GPS, server timestamp, pallet-tag and lot-code OCR, Bluetooth temperature-logger tie-in, a standard shot list built from USDA quality standards, and a signed content-credential manifest. Each load gets a shareable verification link that both parties, a USDA or third-party inspector and PACA arbitrators can open, plus a live tele-inspection mode. Once a rejection is verified, an eight-hour clock starts and alerts go to salvage buyers, processors and food banks.
why_now: By 2026 photo editing with generative tools is trivial and undetectable to most people. The farm labor shortage means late harvests and more variable quality. The EU is moving toward binding food-waste cuts (30% in retail by 2030), which makes measured diversion valuable. Content credentials and device attestation are now standard on phones.
revenue_model: $4-8 per load or $400-1,500 a month per shipper, a 5-8% fee on the recovered value of rerouted salvage, and a co-sell with produce factors who freeze advances during disputes.
non_obvious_insight: In produce, a bad photo is a price-negotiation weapon, and whoever controls the trusted photo controls the money. The wedge is the shipper and the factor, who lose most from doubtful rejections, not the receiver. Verified evidence also turns each rejection from a bargaining event into clean market data.
first_30_days: Offer a free 30-day pilot to 3 grower-shippers in one corridor and capture their next 100 loads. Measure dispute-resolution time before and after. Recruit a produce factoring company or PACA attorney as a co-seller. Build the shot list from USDA grade standards.

title: Landfill Airspace Recovery Contractor
one_liner: Mine old landfill cells to recover airspace, not metals, and sell it to operators at a fraction of the cost of new capacity.
customer: Owners of landfills with under about 10 years of permitted capacity, in airspace-constrained markets: municipal and regional authorities, and independents in the Northeast, Mid-Atlantic and parts of the West.
problem: New landfill cells take years to permit and tipping fees in constrained markets often exceed $100 per ton. Insiders dismiss landfill mining because recovered metals and RDF are low value, so nobody prices the airspace.
solution: An airspace audit (drone LiDAR, borings, waste characterization) followed by a mobile trommel and ballistic-separator spread. It excavates old cells, screens fines for cover and fill, pulls metals and plastics, and re-places compacted residual. Contracts are priced per cubic yard of airspace recovered, compared to the cost of new capacity and haul-out. It skips cells with unknown PFAS risk until sampled.
why_now: Elevated commodity prices, cheaper vision sorting and robotics, tighter EPR and diversion rules that shrink incoming tonnage certainty, and PFAS liability pushing operators to characterize legacy cells anyway.
revenue_model: $25-75K audit fee, then $/CY of airspace recovered (or a share of avoided haul-out cost), plus a share of recovered commodities.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone prices the contents of the landfill. The scarce, regulated, appreciating asset is the airspace, and the true replacement lead time is 10 years.
first_30_days: Screen 20 landfills with under 7 years of remaining capacity using public permit data and satellite volumetrics. Offer free desktop screening and a paid audit of the oldest cell. Lease a trommel by the month rather than buying.

title: Certified SDE for Sub-$1M Business Sales
one_liner: A CPA-signed, AI-prepared earnings certificate that lets brokers, buyers and SBA lenders trust a small business's seller's discretionary earnings.
customer: Business brokers, SBA lenders and first-time buyers in $100k-$1M main-street deals, and the sellers who pay to be believed.
problem: A full quality-of-earnings review costs $15-50k, which is impossible on a $300k deal, so cash-heavy books and owner add-backs create distrust. Deals die in diligence or stall in lender underwriting. Search funds target $5-50M businesses and nothing standardizes trust for the smallest tier.
solution: Upload three years of returns, bank and processor statements and POS data. The system reconstructs revenue, recasts SDE with add-back evidence, and flags unrecorded revenue or personal expenses. A CPA signs a certified SDE range in 48 hours. Partner lenders accept the standard report, and it links to the escrow and route-sale flow.
why_now: SBA 7(a) plus 504 financing up to $10M began July 2026, so buyer demand and lender appetite are rising. LLMs and bank data make the reconstruction cheap.
revenue_model: $495-995 per report paid by the seller or broker, lender licensing, and buyer diligence upsells.
non_obvious_insight: At this size the bottleneck is neither buyers nor capital but trust in the earnings number. A QoE costs 5% of price, and a cheap certificate unlocks the whole tier.
first_30_days: Sign three brokers who list $200k-800k deals and produce 15 reports manually with a CPA. Ask one SBA lender in writing what it needs in order to accept the certificate.

title: Guest-Funded Wildfire Hardening for Vacation Rentals
one_liner: An opt-in per-night 'fire-safe stay' fee that lets guests pay down the ember-proofing of the vacation homes they rent, unlocking insurance credits and renewals for owners who cannot afford the retrofit.
customer: Owners and property managers of vacation rentals and cabins in wildfire-exposed resort towns (Lake Tahoe/Truckee, Big Bear, Mammoth, Idyllwild, Estes Park, Ruidoso, Gatlinburg, Sunriver) facing nonrenewals or multiples of prior premiums. Insurers writing in distressed ZIPs are a secondary payer for leads.
problem: Retrofit baselines run $8K-25K while insurer discounts are only 5-35%, so owners cannot front the cash and the credit is unclaimable in practice. Short-term rentals are the least tolerated use for carriers. Owners are dropped over aerial-imagery roof photos and then have to prove their case. Yet these homes throw off daily cash flow, and their occupants are unfamiliar visitors with the highest life-safety exposure.
solution: An opt-in $3-6 per night fee at checkout (direct-booking sites and partner property managers) pools into a retrofit financing note for that specific house. Vetted crews install ember-resistant vents, roof and gutter fixes and 5-foot-zone clearing to the IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home standard. We build a time-stamped evidence pack (photos, receipts, certificate) and file it with the insurer under the new mitigation-credit and dispute rules. Guests see a public 'hardened home' badge. Owner pays nothing up front, and the fee stream repays the financier over 3-5 years.
why_now: Rules now force insurers to credit and explain: Colorado HB25-1182 has applied since 1 July 2026 (score disclosure, documented-mitigation credit, appeal) and California AB 75 (notice, photo copies, remediation window) went operative 1 July 2026. IBHS Wildfire Prepared Home just expanded to Washington, signaling national scale. California launched a Safe Homes Grant and a revolving loan program. An FTC all-in-pricing rule for short-term lodging (effective May 2025) makes an opt-in structure the clean design.
revenue_model: 15-20% take of the surcharge flow, financing spread on the retrofit note, 3-5% contractor referral fee, and an insurer or MGA lead fee per credited policy or renewal.
non_obvious_insight: A vacation rental is the rare residential asset with a daily, price-insensitive cash stream that can service a retrofit loan, and guests are exactly the people the hardening protects. That aligns payer and beneficiary. Insurers hate short-term rentals most, so documented hardening changes the underwriting conversation where it matters most.
first_30_days: Recruit 10 owners through Big Bear and Truckee property managers. Get one local roofer or vent installer to give fixed-price bids. Add the opt-in fee line through an existing direct-booking tool (Hospitable, OwnerRez or Lodgify style widgets) and measure guest opt-in rate. Line up a $100-250K revenue-based note from a small local lender or angel. File the first evidence packs with two carriers.

title: Capacity-Attested Wishes Recordings for Estate Attorneys
one_liner: Elder-law attorneys add a clinician-scored capacity note and a hash-sealed, attorney-controlled recording of the client's stated wishes to every will or trust signing, so heirs cannot wave the evidence away as a deepfake or as undue influence.
customer: Solo and small-firm elder-law and estate attorneys (they pay per client and mark it up), plus trust companies and bank wealth desks that handle contested-estate risk.
problem: A roughly $6T wealth transfer is under way, probate and estate cases rose about 32% from 2020 to 2024, and the heirs are Gen X and millennial executors. Cheap voice and video cloning means any real recording of 'what Dad said' can now be dismissed as fake, and undue-influence contests keep coming. Many attorneys avoid video because a shaky performance can backfire. Solo agers with no family have nobody to vouch for their wishes at all.
solution: A packaged signing workflow. (1) A 20-minute structured capacity assessment by a telehealth geriatric nurse practitioner or neuropsychologist, timed to the signing day. (2) A guided recording captured in an app that signs at capture with device attestation and a C2PA-style manifest, plus an independent RFC 3161 timestamp. The attorney decides what is retained. (3) An escrow vault that releases to the named executor on receipt of a death certificate. Output is a one-page verification link a probate judge can check without trusting the platform.
why_now: The oldest boomers turned 80 in 2026. FDA-cleared Alzheimer's blood tests (May and Oct 2025) will create a large biomarker-positive but still-competent population whose later wills will be attacked. C2PA 2.3 is mature and TikTok joined in Jul 2026. Voice cloning is good enough that courts and opposing counsel will start treating unsigned recordings as suspect.
revenue_model: $295-495 per client package billed to the law firm (clinician gets about $120, the rest is platform revenue), $99 a month per firm for vault storage and verification links, and later an enterprise tier for trust companies. Long-term escrow storage fees are recurring.
non_obvious_insight: The valuable evidence is not the video. It is a contemporaneous capacity finding made during the pre-dementia 'lucid window' that blood-test diagnosis is about to make very common. Provenance tech simply makes that finding, and the wishes on record, impossible to dismiss as synthetic. Attorneys buy this as malpractice and litigation insurance, not as a media product.
first_30_days: Sign 3 to 5 elder-law firms as design partners through state bar elder-law sections. Contract two geriatric NPs at a per-assessment fee. Build the capture app on off-the-shelf C2PA and timestamping libraries. Run 10 live signings at a discounted $195 and turn each into a case study for the next firm.

title: SNAP Rules Engine for Independent Grocers
one_liner: An API and POS plug-in that classifies every UPC against each state's changing SNAP soda and candy rules.
customer: Independent grocers and convenience stores in states with SNAP restrictions, and the POS and EBT vendors that serve them.
problem: 22 states have SNAP soda and candy restrictions in effect or pending, definitions differ by state, and a June 2026 ruling (Aragon v. Rollins) blocked waivers in five states, so rules keep flipping.
solution: A maintained UPC-level eligibility database by state and effective date, delivered as a POS plug-in and API with audit logs for SNAP authorization defense.
why_now: Patchwork state waivers and court reversals in 2026 mean retailers carry compliance liability without product-level data.
revenue_model: $30-60 per store per month, plus license fees from POS vendors.
non_obvious_insight: Court-driven rule flips make this a recurring data subscription rather than a one-time setup, and the liability sits with retailers who have no tooling.
first_30_days: Classify the top 5,000 UPCs for four states, pilot in 20 independent stores and one POS vendor, and set up a rule-change alert feed.

title: Universal Viva: AI-Run Oral Verification
one_liner: After each major submission the student takes a five-minute identity-verified voice conversation with an AI examiner about their own work, and humans review only the flagged mismatches.
customer: Online and community-college programs, university departments, dual-enrollment providers and credentialing bootcamps (department chairs and deans), later honor councils.
problem: At Harvard 89% of professors received suspected AI work but only 12% referred cases, and 67% say AI hurts their courses. Detectors are unreliable and biased against non-native writers (lower-confidence data). Oral exams work but do not scale: 300 students at 15 minutes each is 75 hours.
solution: A voice agent reads the submission, asks 6-8 adaptive questions on reasoning, sources and choices, checks consistency with the submitted work, and returns a comprehension score. Low-scoring cases go to a bench of trained human examiners. It measures whether the student understands the work rather than accusing anyone of using AI, with accommodations for disabilities and language.
why_now: Real-time voice models with natural turn-taking and low latency matured in 2025-26. Faculty sentiment has turned sharply negative and detection has failed, so institutions need a fairer alternative before the next term's grades.
revenue_model: $3-6 per verification paid by the institution or $30 per student per course, with premium pricing for human audit and site licenses.
non_obvious_insight: Detection asks 'did an AI write this?', which is unanswerable and adversarial. Verification asks 'does the student understand this?', which is answerable, fairer to non-native writers, and much harder to outsource live in a voice conversation.
first_30_days: Pilot with 3 professors in writing-intensive intro courses at a community college, about 60 students. Compare oral-comprehension scores with graded essays and show an instructor dashboard. Move to $4 per verification after the pilot. Set voice-data retention and accessibility policies before launch.

title: Dye-Free SKU Sprints for Walmart Suppliers
one_liner: Fixed-price, eight-week reformulation sprints with pooled colorant supply for mid-size suppliers facing dye deadlines.
customer: Mid-size co-manufacturers, private-label suppliers and regional bakers and candy makers without in-house R&D.
problem: Walmart private label goes dye-free in January 2027 and FDA targets petroleum dye phase-out by December 2027, while reformulation costs $50k-500k per SKU and takes 12-24+ months to validate.
solution: Per-SKU-family sprints covering color matching, stability and shelf-life testing, and access to a pooled natural-colorant supply contract for annatto, butterfly pea and similar inputs.
why_now: Products with FD&C dyes are about 4% of items but $57.8B in sales, natural colorant demand is projected to rise 400-500%, and the US is 98% import-dependent for annatto.
revenue_model: $25-60k per SKU family plus margin on pooled colorant supply.
non_obvious_insight: Validation is the bottleneck rather than ideas. A shared test lab and pooled purchasing let mid-size firms without R&D meet the deadline that big brands will already have met.
first_30_days: Interview 20 private-label suppliers to Walmart, offer a discounted first sprint to three, and line up one colorant supplier and one contract lab.

title: Findings Sentinel: A Nurse Tracks Your Scan Follow-Ups
one_liner: What a concierge doctor really sells is closed loops: someone reads every report and owns the follow-up; for $20/mo, a nurse-in-the-loop sentinel makes sure your incidental scan findings do not fall through the cracks.
customer: Adults 50-80 (and their adult children) who had a CT, MRI, ultrasound or pathology in the last three years. Incidentals include lung nodules, thyroid, adrenal and kidney lesions, pancreatic cysts and aneurysms. Secondary buyers are self-insured employers, Medicare Advantage plans and imaging centers that carry follow-up liability.
problem: Studies of incidental findings report follow-up failure rates commonly in the 30-60% range (lung nodules especially). The ordering physician is often not notified beyond the report, the PCP is not copied, and under the Cures Act patients see results in portals before anyone explains them. A concierge doctor reads everything and calls; everyone else gets an unread PDF.
solution: Pull records through patient-directed access (Medicare App Library apps, Apple Health Records, portals) or PDF upload. An LLM extracts each 'recommend follow-up in X months' statement and tracks whether it happened. An RN or NP reviews flagged items and issues a plain-language one-pager with the question to ask and a drafted message or referral request to the PCP. A monthly digest and annual records reconciliation are included. No diagnosis or prescribing, so it is navigation, not telemedicine.
why_now: CMS's Health Tech Ecosystem launched its Medicare App Library in April 2026 with hundreds of organizations pledged to FHIR-based sharing, and TEFCA-style patient access is maturing. LLMs are reliable at extracting follow-up recommendations from radiology text, the same technique hospital nodule programs use. That makes nurse minutes rare and targeted.
revenue_model: $20/mo membership; $99 one-time 'catch-up review' of the last three years; $2-4 per member per month from employers and Medicare Advantage plans; imaging centers pay for closed-loop follow-up as risk reduction. Rough cost basis: extraction costs pennies and, if about 8% of members are flagged yearly at about 25 nurse minutes, clinical labor is only a few dollars per member per year.
non_obvious_insight: The concierge doctor's value is not the 60-minute visit; it is that a competent person reads every report and owns the loop. Loop closure is an insurance-like utilization problem: about 95% of members have nothing to flag most months, so the pooled cost fits $20/mo. Immediate-release results created a new market for 'someone to tell me what this means and what happens next'.
first_30_days: Manually pilot with 30 volunteers recruited from incidentaloma communities and senior centers. Members upload reports, a contract RN reviews them, and you count unclosed loops. Publish the results ('X% had an unclosed loop') for PR, and use them to sign one imaging center or employer pilot before building the app.

title: Teleoperated Pack-and-Pick Robots Piloted from Latin America
one_liner: Robot arms run by foundation models, with remote pilots in Guatemala or Colombia fixing the edge cases, sold per box.
customer: Berry, tomato and cucumber packhouses and greenhouses that lost crews.
problem: Farm labor shrank by at least 155,000 and crews were lost in 2026 harvests, while robots pick at 50-60% of human speed and fail on edge cases.
solution: Rent arms with a vision-language-action stack for clamshell packing, and route failures to remote operators at roughly one pilot per 8-10 arms, priced per case.
why_now: Physical-AI models matured in 2025-26, remote-assist tooling and satellite or 5G links are cheap, and enforcement removed the informal labor pool.
revenue_model: Per-case fee with a minimum monthly commitment per station.
non_obvious_insight: Robots run about 20 hours a day at half human speed, and remote humans fix the rare failures. The result is a labor channel that needs neither a visa nor a robot that never fails.
first_30_days: Rent two arms, set up a clamshell-packing station at one packhouse, and hire three remote operators for a paid pilot.

title: Wearable-Triggered Spending Guardrails for Sports Bettors
one_liner: A debit card and betting-budget wallet that tightens gambling, day-trading and BNPL limits automatically when the wearer's sleep, heart-rate variability and late-night pattern predict impulsive decisions, with an optional spouse or sponsor as co-guardian.
customer: US adults who bet legally on sports or prediction markets and want limits: self-referred users, partners and recovery groups first. Credit unions and employer assistance programs are the B2B2C channel. The price is $6-9 a month.
problem: Roughly 40 states have legal sports betting and sports prediction contracts have spread. Household credit stress is at record levels, with delinquencies at highs and deposits often funded by cards or BNPL. Existing blocks are all-or-nothing, and willpower fails at 2 a.m. after a losing streak. A wearable knows when the user is depleted, but the bank has never seen that signal.
solution: An issued card and ledger, built on a card-issuing platform, that funds a weekly betting wallet. The user pre-commits the rules when calm. If sleep drops below a set threshold, HRV falls against baseline, or two late-night losses stack up, the wallet enters a 24-hour cooldown, cuts the daily cap, or asks a partner to approve top-ups. Wearable sync is opt-in via Oura, Whoop, Garmin or Apple Health. Only a one-bit cooldown flag leaves the phone.
why_now: Legal betting and prediction-market sports contracts scaled through 2025-26. Brazil banned online betting and announced debt relief on Sept 25, 2026, showing the politics have turned. The CFPB open-banking rule is stayed and unstable, so a business built on card-level controls avoids dependence on aggregator data. Wearables are now mainstream, with Whoop raising $575M this year.
revenue_model: $7 a month subscription plus interchange share. Credit unions and neobanks license it for $1-2 per member per month. State problem-gambling councils pay for evidence-based tools. Anything sold to sportsbooks is optional and kept separate to avoid conflicts.
non_obvious_insight: Financial products treat every hour as equal, but behavior is not. The best predictor of a regretted transaction is the user's physiological state at 1 a.m., which the user's own wearable measures and the bank never sees. Sell control, not surveillance: the user writes the rules in advance and a bank never sees raw health data.
first_30_days: Ship a no-card MVP: an SMS and Slack bot that uses the Oura or Whoop API to send cooldown alerts, plus a partner-approval flow. Recruit 50 users from recovering-bettor communities. Measure whether cooldowns cut after-midnight deposits. Then pilot with one credit union that already offers gambling merchant-category blocks, and price at $7 a month.

title: Step-Down Club: Maintenance After the Max Dose
one_liner: A cheap maintenance membership that turns the majority of GLP-1 users who quit or plateau into a planned step-down and a monetizable restart.
customer: Adults 3-12 months into a cash-pay GLP-1 who have hit goal or are about to quit over cost (consumer pays); telehealths and pharmacies pay a bounty per verified restart.
problem: About one-third of non-diabetic obesity patients are still on therapy at 1 year. Stoppers regain roughly 4x faster than people who lost weight with behavior change, and ~60% of ex-users say they intend to restart. Every company optimizes for staying on the max dose, and nobody sells the middle path or owns the ex-user.
solution: At plateau, a physician-written protocol steps the user down to the lowest effective dose or a planned holiday. A connected scale plus waist and strength check-ins run on SMS. Pre-agreed regain triggers (e.g. +3% above nadir for 2 consecutive weeks) auto-route the user to the cheapest legitimate restart, such as a $149 pill program. Optional 'regain warranty' credit as an add-on.
why_now: SURMOUNT-MAINTAIN (Lancet, 2026) is the first RCT showing a reduced 5 mg tirzepatide dose kept about 70% of the weight loss (-16.6% vs -21.9% at max dose vs -9.9% on placebo). $149-$299 pills (Wegovy pill Jan 2026, Foundayo Apr 2026) make restart cheap. Telehealths are converging on the same price and now compete on acquisition cost.
revenue_model: $19-29/month membership, plus $75-150 partner bounty per verified restart or step-down conversion (a telehealth's first-fill CAC is est. $150-400), plus optional warranty add-on.
non_obvious_insight: Discontinuation is the modal outcome, not a failure mode. A restart is a lead worth more than the membership fee, so whoever owns the ex-user relationship owns the cheapest reacquisition channel in a market where every competitor sells the same drug at the same price.
first_30_days: Recruit 100 plateaued or ex-users from r/Zepbound, r/Semaglutide and Facebook groups. Have an obesity-medicine MD write the step-down and restart protocol. Run the check-ins on SMS with a BYO or $25 scale. Sign one telehealth or pharmacy partner for a per-restart bounty. Charge $19/month from day one.

title: Shelved-Game Rescue Exchange
one_liner: A broker that packages cancelled and orphaned game prototypes and licenses them to laid-off veteran teams on revenue-share terms, with reversion rights if the game stalls.
customer: Publishers, closing studios and insolvency administrators holding unreleased builds (they get a recovery instead of a write-off). The paying counterparties are veteran-led small teams and the funders behind them.
problem: Ubisoft cancelled six games in Jan 2026 and cut headcount from 18,666 to 16,590. EA's owners closed a $55B LBO with $20B of debt and a stated plan to cut costs with AI. Cancelled projects sit unused with teams disbanded, while laid-off veterans have skills but no IP or prototype budget.
solution: Build a 'prototype data room' per project: build, design docs, and a third-party licence and music clearance audit. Add a standard rescue licence (revenue share, milestone reversion, credit terms) and a registry of veteran team leads. Match the two, and offer milestone-funded finishing through a small fund or partner investors. Start with insolvent and small publishers, which move faster than Ubisoft or EA legal.
why_now: The 2023-26 layoff wave left an unusually deep bench of finished-quality talent. The EA LBO and Ubisoft restructuring guarantee more shelved work. Steam distribution and Epic's 0% fee on the first $1M make a 10-20 person finish economically viable.
revenue_model: 10-15% of the licensee's revenue share, or a success fee at signing ($10-50k), plus a data-room packaging fee paid by the rights holder.
non_obvious_insight: A shelved game's cost to its owner is legal and opportunity overhead, not the code. A zero-upfront licence with reversion beats a write-down and avoids a public fire sale. Insiders assume cancelled means bad, but many projects die for portfolio or budget-cycle reasons, not quality.
first_30_days: Publish a public 'orphaned prototypes wanted' page. Call 20 insolvency administrators and mid-size publishers found through recent studio-closure announcements with a one-page offer. Have a games lawyer draft the rescue licence. Recruit 10 veteran-led teams from layoff communities on Discord and LinkedIn. Aim for one signed rescue by day 60.

title: Independent Safety Registry for Pet Medicines
one_liner: A neutral post-market surveillance system for veterinary drugs and biologics, built on pet-insurance claims plus owner-reported outcomes.
customer: Animal-health drugmakers and biologics developers (safety and medical-affairs teams) pay subscriptions. Pet insurers and MGAs pay for cost-effectiveness analytics. Vet groups and foundations use the public lookup.
problem: Vet adverse-event reporting is voluntary and underreported, and after the 2025 controversy over reported adverse events with anti-NGF antibody injections for canine osteoarthritis, owners and vets have no independent way to weigh safety signals. Pharma-run surveillance is not trusted. Insurers hold the only longitudinal cross-clinic data, yet are pushing 19.7% premium increases on 9% more animals without knowing which treatments reduce downstream claims. New modalities (mAbs, CGMs, long-acting insulins, oral oncology, and possibly a canine longevity drug) are arriving with no owner for outcomes data.
solution: A data trust that ingests de-identified claims from partner insurers and MGAs, optional practice-management extracts, and owner-reported outcomes gathered by a QR code at the clinic. It runs disproportionality signal detection in the style of FDA Sentinel. Outputs are (a) a safety dashboard for drug makers, (b) formulary and cost-effectiveness reports for insurers, and (c) a public 'what happened to dogs like mine' lookup for vets and owners.
why_now: Premiums rose 19.7% against 9% more animals, so insurers need loss-control insight. Big biologics and Loyal's longevity program (1,317 dogs in the STAY study, FDA acceptance of efficacy and safety sections) mean a wave of new launches. IDEXX buying CoVet shows workflow data is becoming a strategic asset, and independent players need a neutral alternative.
revenue_model: Pharma subscriptions of $60-250k per product family per year. Insurer analytics contracts of $50-150k per year. Custom post-marketing studies at $100-300k. A free public tier drives owner-reported data.
non_obvious_insight: Companion-animal medicine is the last big therapeutic area with no Sentinel-style system, and insurers are the only long-lived holders of cross-clinic data. After a public safety scare, drugmakers will pay for credibility that they cannot generate themselves, and insurers will pay for the same data to reduce claims.
first_30_days: Pitch small MGAs and startup insurers (hungry for analytics, less locked into data rules) on a free pilot in exchange for a data-sharing agreement. Build signal detection for the 10 most common drugs and biologics. Publish a public report on one hot topic, then sell two pharma safety leads a pilot subscription. Expect first revenue at month 4-6.

title: Real-Brine Library and DLE Benchmark Lab
one_liner: A neutral bank of characterised real brines, matrix-matched reference materials and public bake-offs of direct lithium extraction vendors, so nobody has to run a $3M private pilot to compare technologies.
customer: Three payers. First, brine developers (Smackover, Salton Sea geothermal, Argentine and Chilean salars, Utah and Nevada, Canadian oilfield brines) buying screening reports of $15-40k. Second, DLE vendors paying $30-80k per benchmark round for credible independent data. Third, commercial labs paying $2-3k per year for proficiency testing and buying CRMs.
problem: DLE vendors demonstrate on synthetic or 'friendly' brines. Real brines differ in Mg, Ca, Fe, Mn, silica, organics, H2S and temperature. Sorbent life, water balance and reagent cost only show up after hundreds of cycles, so every developer runs its own bespoke pilot ($1-5M, 12-18 months), and claims cannot be compared. On top of that, high-TDS brines (200-400 g/L) are notoriously hard to assay. Different labs disagree by 5-15% because of matrix effects, so 'recovery' computed from assay is shaky. Sealed drums of characterised brine from finished pilots sit unused in every developer's yard.
solution: Collect 12-20 characterised brines, anonymised if the owner wishes, stabilised in sealed drums. Run standardised bench protocols with vendors (50-100 sorption and desorption cycles, membrane or solvent equivalents) and publish scorecards on Li recovery, Mg and Ca rejection, water use, reagent cost per tonne LCE and degradation curve. Sell matrix-matched brine CRMs and inter-laboratory proficiency rounds to labs, and publish a certified-lab list. Developers buy cheap 'technology screening' reports that shortlist vendors before committing to a pilot. Lenders' independent engineers cite the benchmark.
why_now: After the 2023-25 lithium price collapse, investors will only fund bankable, independently verified technology. A wave of DLE technology-selection decisions is happening now in the Smackover, Argentina (RIGI-backed projects), Chile and geothermal brines. The vendor field is crowded and undifferentiated, so vendors will pay for third-party proof.
revenue_model: Vendor benchmark fees ($30-80k per brine set), developer report subscriptions ($15-40k per year), CRM sales, and proficiency-test scheme fees ($2-3k per lab per year), plus certification.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone thinks DLE is a chemistry problem. In practice it is a brine-specific reliability and data-credibility problem, and no one has standard reference brines, so every claim is unfalsifiable. The killers are minor components (silica, organics, Fe and Mn oxidation) that wreck sorbents after 200 cycles, which a fast pilot on an easy brine never shows. The insider knows that the leftover barrel is the asset.
first_30_days: Ask five friendly developers and labs for 20 L of retained brine (leftover after pilots). Characterise each with two labs. Invite three DLE vendors to co-fund a bake-off on one shared brine. Sell an inter-laboratory round to 6 labs at $2k each (about $12k in the first month) and pre-sell a $10k screening report to 3 developers. Publish the interlab bias chart as the marketing piece.

title: Batteries That Pay Off Utility Arrears
one_liner: Install free home batteries in households behind on bills and let capacity payments retire the debt, which is cheaper for the utility than writing it off.
customer: Utilities, co-ops and munis in high-capacity-price regions (PJM first) that run arrears and shutoff programs. State PUCs and community action agencies co-sponsor. The utility pays from bad-debt and program budgets.
problem: 13.4M households were disconnected in 2024 and about 1 in 6 are behind on bills. Rates rose 7.3% in a year and this is a midterm issue. At the $325/MW-day cap, each kW of dispatchable capacity is worth about $118 a year, so a 5 kW home battery is worth roughly $590 a year gross, before accreditation haircuts and the aggregator's share.
solution: A no-cost 10 kWh 'bill-relief battery' for arrears households, enrolled in a utility or aggregator capacity program. Capacity and energy revenue is credited against the arrears balance for 5-7 years, after which the customer keeps it or the utility retains it. The company handles installation, financing and dispatch. The utility gets less bad debt and fewer politically toxic shutoffs.
why_now: Capacity prices hit the cap, packs cost about $70/kWh, dispatch at scale is proven, and utilities are under political pressure on affordability with few tools.
revenue_model: Per-install fee, a share of capacity revenue while the arrears are being retired, utility program payments, and project finance spread.
non_obvious_insight: At this capacity price, a battery earns more than it costs to give one away. Utility bad debt is a hidden capex budget that has never been spent on assets.
first_30_days: Get one utility's arrears distribution and model unit economics under current capacity prices. Pitch five community action agencies and three co-ops or munis on a 50-home pilot funded by weatherization-adjacent money. Line up a philanthropic first-loss guarantee.

title: Contingency Royalty Audits for Game Developers
one_liner: A $99 automated statement check that finds provable underpayments in publisher royalty reports, then hands winnable cases to forensic accountants on contingency.
customer: Developers signed with publishers who are unrecouped or getting opaque quarterly statements. They pay $99-299 for the check and 20-25% of any recovered money. Referral fees also come from games lawyers and auditors.
problem: Audit clauses exist in most publishing deals (one analysis found them in 88% of deals with an advance), but a formal audit costs more than a small studio can recover, so publishers effectively face none. One 30-contract analysis found 42% gave the publisher 100% of revenue until recoupment. Marketing 'recoupables', vague net-revenue definitions, cross-collateralization and FX and VAT handling all hide errors. Devs sit on a spreadsheet they can't verify.
solution: Devs upload the contract and statements. We rebuild the recoup waterfall from the contract's own definitions and compare it with independent signals: review-count unit estimates, price history and regional mix. We flag anomalies such as marketing above a cap, taxes deducted twice, giveaway keys counted as spend, and FX gaps. A clause pack and a negotiation script push new deals toward Steamworks read-only financial permission for the dev. Flagged cases go to a panel of forensic accountants who send a formal audit notice.
why_now: The 2023-25 layoffs pushed thousands of devs into 'marketing-only' publishing deals with recoup terms. LLMs can now parse contracts and statements at near-zero marginal cost. Funding is tight, so every unpaid royalty matters.
revenue_model: Flat pre-audit fee, 20-25% contingency on recoveries (cheaper than the roughly 40% litigation contingency), and referral fees from lawyers. Later: a paid tier for funds and lenders that want portfolio royalty monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: Detection was never the bottleneck. Cost was. A cheap pre-audit that separates provable errors from noise lets an auditor take only winnable cases. Publishers in a small, gossipy industry often settle quickly once a credible notice lands, because they don't want the precedent to spread, and many errors are honest spreadsheet mistakes.
first_30_days: Launch a free recoup-waterfall calculator and a 'publisher-deal red-flag scan' on r/gamedev and dev Discords. Collect about 100 anonymized statements as training and proof data. Sign referral deals with two games-industry lawyers and one forensic accountant. Take the first 5 contingency cases with flagged anomalies over $10k.

title: Childcare Credits Instead of Builder Rate Buydowns
one_liner: Homebuilders replace temporary mortgage rate buydowns with redeemable childcare credits, and the program builds the licensed care space inside the community.
customer: Small and mid-size spec and production builders with unsold inventory in family-heavy exurbs (Sunbelt and Midwest), and master-planned community developers. The end buyers are young families with kids under 5.
problem: 63% of builders use incentives and 80-90% of new-home sales need rate buydowns with 30-year rates near 7%, yet completions fell 27.1% year over year. Buydowns are a one-time cost that fades in 2-3 years. For a household with toddlers, childcare ($13,128 per child, more than a mortgage for two kids in 45 states) is the actual affordability wall, and new suburbs are childcare deserts.
solution: The builder funds a Family Care Credit (for example $400 a month for 24 months) redeemable only at licensed providers in a vetted network. The startup pre-commits reserved occupancy with providers and helps a provider open in the community, using a builder-built care-ready clubhouse room, flex unit or model home at cost. The credit's cost accrues only when used, so expected builder spend can undercut a $12-20K buydown. Marketing kit: 'move-in ready, childcare included'.
why_now: Incentives are at a cyclical high, starts are steady but completions fell 27.1% and builders are financing shops. ROAD to Housing Act streamlining for small multifamily and factory-built homes aims at exactly these family starter products. Dependent-care FSA limits rose to $7,500, and childcare deserts are politically salient.
revenue_model: 10-15% program fee on credit dollars funded by the builder, per-family placement fee from providers, and later a margin on prepaid-slot financing.
non_obvious_insight: Builders see incentives as price cuts, but a family with a toddler values $400 a month of childcare more than a temporary rate cut. A builder is already a construction company, so converting a room to licensed space costs them little and is worth a rent-free facility to a provider. The guaranteed occupancy is what makes the provider's economics work in the first place.
first_30_days: Target five small builders with spec inventory in fast-growing exurbs. Check local childcare deserts with the CAP map, sign one builder for a 10-home pilot, and line up two licensed home providers. Launch a 'move-in ready with childcare' landing page and compare lead conversion to the builder's buydown ads. Have counsel confirm the credit's treatment against buyer-concession rules.

title: Age-Signal Rules Engine for App Developers
one_liner: A 'feature-flag service for minors' law': an SDK that takes the OS or app-store age bracket plus jurisdiction and returns the legally required feature set, with citations and an audit trail.
customer: Mid-size consumer apps, games and edtech (10-500 staff) with under-18 users, their general counsel, and app agencies. Series A-C startups first.
problem: Texas app-store age verification (June 2026), Ohio consent (June 2026), Florida under-14 ban, California's OS age-attestation law, the UK regime, and bans in Australia, Brazil, Indonesia and Malaysia each define brackets and required behavior differently. Engineers hard-code rules and rules change monthly. Fines are large.
solution: A versioned policy graph maintained by lawyers plus LLM change tracking. The SDK returns flags for chat, DMs, push timing, ads, purchases and recommendation feeds per bracket and jurisdiction. It integrates with OS age-range signals and third-party verifiers and logs which rule applied when, for regulators.
why_now: For the first time OS and app stores hand developers an age signal (California signed Oct 2025; Apple and Google age-range APIs, from memory), but nobody says what to do with it. The 'policy ratchet' means fragmentation will grow.
revenue_model: $500-5k a month by MAU tier, plus one-time compliance-matrix audits at $3-6k.
non_obvious_insight: Age-verification vendors sell the signal, and nobody sells the decision: the legal mapping from signal to product behavior. That mapping is the durable moat because laws keep diverging.
first_30_days: Publish a public 8-jurisdiction by 5-feature matrix. Run a newsletter around it. Sell 5 compliance-matrix audits at $4k to game and app teams. Wrap the logic into an SDK by month 3.
